title: Two Equal Disjoint Squares
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `N` and `M`.
Each of the next `N` lines contains a string of `M` characters, each `0` or `1`, describing one row of the map.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum side length, or `0` if two squares cannot be placed.

examples.explanation: The squares with top-left cells (0, 0) and (2, 3), both of side 2, cover only buildable cells and share no cell. Side 3 is impossible: a 3 x 3 block of ones needs three buildable rows and columns, and the grid has no room for two disjoint ones.
The grid is entirely buildable, but two disjoint squares of side 3 would need 6 rows or 6 columns, and only 5 exist. Two squares of side 2 fit, for example at the top-left and bottom-right corners.
There is only one buildable cell, so two non-overlapping squares cannot be placed and the answer is 0.

hints: If two disjoint squares of side `s` exist, then two disjoint squares of side `s - 1` exist as well, so the answer can be found by searching over `s` from large to small (or by binary search).
Compute, for every cell, the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is that cell. A square of side `s` fits with that corner exactly when the value is at least `s`.

Two squares of side `s` with corners `(r1, c1)` and `(r2, c2)` are disjoint exactly when `|r1 - r2| >= s` or `|c1 - c2| >= s`. The largest such difference over all valid corners is determined by the smallest and largest valid row and column, so you only need the per-row and per-column maxima of the DP table.
